title: Ubisoft – creativity, crisis and a family empire (Klausur 2025)
text: Ubisoft was founded in 1986 by the five Guillemot brothers, sons of a family of farm suppliers in Brittany. Starting with the distribution of software, they turned it into one of the largest video game publishers in the world, with franchises such as Assassin's Creed, Far Cry, Just Dance, Rainbow Six, Prince of Persia and the Rabbids. The family still controls the group; Yves Guillemot has been CEO since its creation. Between 2015 and 2018 the brothers fought off a hostile takeover attempt by Vivendi, a story the company tells as proof of its independence. Its stated mission is to enrich players' lives by creating original and memorable gaming experiences.

At its peak in 2022, Ubisoft employed around 20,000 people in some 45 studios on every continent; Ubisoft Montreal alone has several thousand employees. Big games are made in co-development: a lead studio steers the project and up to a dozen other studios produce parts of it – cities, missions, multiplayer modes, testing. Teams of programmers, artists, game designers and writers work in sprints and must reach milestones. Studios share in-house game engines and tools (Anvil, Snowdrop) and common production processes. All projects are validated at each stage by the Editorial department at the Paris headquarters, led for many years by the Chief Creative Officer Serge Hascoët, who had the final word on every game. Critics and players speak of a “Ubisoft formula”: open worlds built with the same recipe of towers to climb, maps full of icons and similar side missions.

Employees describe a passionate, young and informal environment, proud of iconic games, and a “family” company. Salaries, however, are often below those of other tech companies, crunch periods before launches are frequent and careers depend heavily on one's project. In the summer of 2020, dozens of testimonies published on social media and in the French press revealed sexual harassment and a culture of humiliation, especially within the Paris Editorial team, described as a “boys' club” where star creators were untouchable and HR protected managers. Serge Hascoët, the head of Ubisoft Canada and the global head of HR resigned; other managers were dismissed. Ubisoft announced a new code of conduct, an anonymous alert line, diversity targets and hired a new Chief People Officer. In 2025, a French court gave three former executives suspended prison sentences for harassment.

Since 2022, Ubisoft has been in financial difficulty: delayed and cancelled games, disappointing sales and a collapsing share price. The group launched cost-cutting plans, closed studios and cut several thousand jobs. In France, employees went on strike in 2024 over wages and against a new rule requiring more days of presence at the office. In 2025 the Chinese group Tencent invested about 1.2 billion euros for a minority stake in a new subsidiary grouping Assassin's Creed, Far Cry and Rainbow Six.
